newsitem.title: Austria: OSCE says cannot check Serbia elections.
newsitem.headline: OSCE says cannot check Serbia elections.

text.p: Yugoslavia on Friday invited Europe's security forum to send a delegation to Belgrade to discuss disputed local elections, but officials said the terms of the invitation meant it would be unable to verify the results of the polls.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) welcomed a request from Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic to obtain what he called the "true information" on the elections, which took place nearly a month ago.
Milutinovic wrote that the invitation had been made "due to dissatisfaction with the election results and the protests staged by a part of the opposition", the OSCE said.
The OSCE's outgoing chairman-in-office, Swiss Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti, said he would give serious consideration to the request from Belgrade.
"He believes this invitation could open up the possibility for dialogue. He will respond to the request soon," the OSCE said in a statement.

But OSCE chief spokeswoman Melissa Fleming said nowhere in the letter was the body called on to check the results of the elections, in which the Zajedno opposition said the socialists suffered their worst defeat in 50 years of unbroken rule.
"The OSCE will not be in a position to go to the country and verify the results of the election," she told Reuters.

"What the OSCE could do is send a high-level delegation to meet all interested parties, with the condition that the OSCE has open access to all of them and to make recommendations following that on ways to get out of the crisis," she added.
One Western diplomatic source in Vienna earlier warned the OSCE to tread carefully to avoid being manipulated by Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.
Milosevic has come under severe diplomatic criticism from the West over his refusal to accept opposition victories in local elections in Serbia on November 17.

Thousands of people have poured on to the streets of Belgrade for the past three weeks in peaceful protests after the authorities overturned results in Belgrade and other towns claimed by the opposition, citing unspecified "irregularities".
The diplomatic source said it was very unlikely OSCE experts could verify a vote which took place a month ago.
"Anything could have happened to the ballots in that time," the source said. "Checking the election in that way would serve no purpose."
The 54-member organisation, which joins all European states with the United States and Canada, said it had no problem sending a delegation to Belgrade despite Yugoslavia's suspension from the body.
Yugoslavia -- comprising Serbia and Montenegro -- had its membership of the OSCE suspended in 1992 after Belgrade was accused of stoking the war in neighbouring Bosnia.

Another Western diplomat said the only recommendation open to the OSCE would be to advise Milosevic to re-run the elections with a full team of observers from the forum to monitor the polls, a possible solution to enable Milosevic to save face.
